dedupe_keys.name: knight capital trading incident 2012 and sec enforcement order

description: This case study is the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's enforcement action over the Knight Capital trading incident of 1 August 2012, in which a defective deployment of new code, combined with dormant legacy code, made the firm's automated equity order router send more than 4 million orders into the market in the first 45 minutes of trading while trying to fill 212 customer orders. Knight traded 397 million shares, built positions worth billions and lost more than $460 million. The SEC announced charges and a $12 million settlement on 16 October 2013, and its full administrative order is a free PDF. Caveats: the order is a settled enforcement document, so it presents the SEC's findings without a trial and focuses on compliance, not market-wide effects. It found that Knight violated the Market Access Rule (Rule 15c3-5) by lacking adequate controls on order entry, risk limits, code deployment and review, and also breached short sale rules. For simulation it is a well-documented case of a software fault cascading into a near-failure of a market participant within minutes, useful for operational resilience and cascading failure studies of trading infrastructure. It is related to the TSB IT migration failure record in this catalogue, another IT-driven failure in finance.
